introduction: “Words must be supported by deeds, for deeds are the true test of words.” This guide follows that sentence through Bahá’u’lláh’s tablets and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s talks: faith is proved by conduct, a teacher is believed for what he does, good character is an army stronger than swords, and nothing done for the sake of God is lost. A hundred of the guide’s 210 quotations are given here, ten from each tenth of its length. Beside them stand a hundred voices from elsewhere: James against faith without works, the Sermon on the Mount, the Qur’an on the deeds that endure, Confucius and Marcus Aurelius, Chaucer’s parson, Portia’s candle. About one in five pulls another way and ends in a question: Paul on faith without the deeds of the law, the command to give alms in secret, Machiavelli on unarmed prophets, Antony and Shelley on what is remembered.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says faith “does not consist in belief, it consists in deeds”; Paul says a man is justified by faith and not by works. What is each of them guarding against?
The readings ask that deeds be seen, so that people may find their Source; Jesus asks that alms be hidden from one’s own left hand. When should a good deed be visible?
Deeds are judged by their motives, and yet only deeds can be seen. Samuel was told that the Lord looks on the heart. How should we read one another’s conduct?
Good character is called sharper than swords. Machiavelli says unarmed prophets are destroyed. What examples would you bring on either side?
The guide promises that no deed done for God is lost. Antony, Shelley and the Preacher doubt that anything good is remembered. What would it change in your day to believe the promise?
Portia can more easily teach twenty what is good than be one of the twenty to follow it. Where is that true of you, and what has ever closed the gap?

outside.why: “Words must be supported by deeds, for deeds are the true test of words.” James is the New Testament’s bluntest voice for it: faith without works is dead.
Bahá’u’lláh makes deeds the test of words. Emerson would not let the two be parted: words are also actions, and actions are a kind of words. When is a word itself the deed that is wanted?
“An act, however infinitesimal, is … mightier than a mountain.” The Qur’an gives the same scale: whoso doeth good an atom’s weight will see it.
“Love manifests its reality in deeds, not only in words.” John’s letter: let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.

“Make not your deeds as snares wherewith to entrap the object of your aspiration.” Jesus warns against a nearer snare, alms done to be seen of men. What is the difference between doing good to gain heaven and doing it to gain applause?
“All that are on earth shall pass away, while good deeds alone shall endure.” The Qur’an says the same against wealth and children: the good deeds which endure are better.
“Say not that which thou doest not.” The Qur’an asks believers the same thing as a question: why say ye that which ye do not?
“One’s righteous deeds testify to the truth of one’s words.” Jesus’ test for any teacher: by their fruits ye shall know them.

To admit that health is good is not health, says ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, and concludes that a physician is needed. Portia knows the gap from inside: she can easier teach twenty what were good to be done than be one of the twenty. Why is knowing so much easier?
Acknowledging that honour is excellent “does not make a man honorable”. Aristotle on the same evasion: most people take refuge in theory and think they will become good that way.
Those who say what they do not practise are compared to people who said “God is our Lord” and then denied Him. Jesus: why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?
“Mere acceptance of the Cause … is not and hath never been sufficient.” The Sermon on the Mount: not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter.
All make the claim, and their conduct gives them the lie. Paul to Titus: they profess that they know God; but in works they deny him.
“The inward without the outward is deficient, and belief without deeds is void.” James: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls belief without deeds void. Paul concludes that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law, and Luther built a church on the sentence. What was Paul afraid deeds would become?
Faith is hidden; “its proof lies in deeds and conduct”. Confucius changed his own practice on this point: now my way is to hear their words, and look at their conduct.
“Deeds are as mirrors wherein the reality of the doer is revealed.” Jesus uses a tree for the same thought: the tree is known by his fruit.
“The doer is known by his deeds, not his words.” Proverbs says it holds from the start: even a child is known by his doings.
“The quality of man lies in his conduct and deeds.” Marcus Aurelius to himself: no longer talk about the kind of man a good man ought to be, but be such.

“Look ye at every soul according to their deeds and behavior.” Samuel, choosing a king, is told that man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart. How far can anyone judge another by what is seen?
“They should justify their claim to be Bahá’ís by deeds and not by name.” Carlyle: conviction, were it never so excellent, is worthless till it convert itself into conduct.
Not by lip-service “but by patient lives of active service” have the elect brought light. Shimon ben Gamliel, raised among sages: not study is the chief thing, but action.
“Faith does not consist in belief, it consists in deeds.” Paul himself, a chapter before his teaching on faith: not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers.
Faith, in this talk, consists in deeds. Paul to the Ephesians: by grace are ye saved through faith, not of works, lest any man should boast. What does a faith defined by deeds do with boasting?
“Whatever a man’s tongue speaketh, that let him prove by his deeds.” Ophelia to her brother: do not show me the thorny way to heaven and tread the primrose path yourself.
A believer’s claim is proved by acting on it. Chaucer’s country parson is the pattern in English: first he wrought, and afterward he taught.
None can claim relationship to Bahá’u’lláh except those who follow His example in deeds. Jesus, told that his family was outside: whosoever shall do the will of my Father, the same is my brother.
“Let him then who hopeth to attain the presence of his Lord work a righteous work.” Bahá’u’lláh is quoting this verse of the Qur’an.
Good deeds that do not spring from the love of God “will be imperfect”. Paul: though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.

Deeds are complete only with the knowledge and love of God. Leigh Hunt’s Abou, not on the list of those who love the Lord, asks to be written as one who loves his fellow men, and his name leads all the rest. Which way does the dependence run?
After recognition, “all must act according to that which hath been sent down in the Book”. Jesus ends his sermon on the same condition: whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them.

Deeds and their acceptance depend, “in the first instance”, on something beyond the deed. Isaiah puts the dependence at its hardest: all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags. What keeps that thought from discouraging the doer?
“Deeds are not accepted except through turning towards God.” Jesus on what the doer may claim afterwards: we are unprofitable servants; we have done that which was our duty.
“Blessed is the soul whose outward life is the same as its inward life.” Jesus’ image for the other case: whited sepulchres, beautiful outward and within full of dead men’s bones.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá cites this tradition from “the previous Dispensation”. It is the first saying in the chief Sunni collection.

Deeds are judged by their motives. Krishna names the motive to be rid of: let right deeds be thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them. How does that sit with the rewards promised to good deeds elsewhere in this guide?
“The days when idle worship was deemed sufficient are ended.” Amos said it in God’s name of the feast days and solemn assemblies: let judgment run down as waters.
Only pure motive supported by pure deeds is acceptable. Hosea’s line, which Jesus quoted twice: I desired mercy, and not sacrifice.
“If We perceive from them the sweet smelling savor of purity and holiness, We will most certainly bless you.” Paul uses the same sense: we are unto God a sweet savour.

Love for all religions is to be shown “through deeds and not through the tongue”. Pope went further: for modes of faith let graceless zealots fight; his can’t be wrong whose life is in the right. Is that where this guide leads, or somewhere short of it?
Asked the best way to spread the teaching: “By deeds … Join yourselves to those who work for the poor, the weak and the unfortunate.” Jesus counts each such deed as done to him.
Deeds are understood by all. James’s definition of religion needs no translation: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction.
The test of a belief is whether “it makes us kind and loving in our relations with our fellow-men”. Jesus gave the same test for his disciples: by this shall all men know.
If it makes us kind, it is true. William Penn: the humble, meek, merciful, just, pious and devout souls are everywhere of one religion.
“Good deeds are accepted by all nations and religions.” Peter: in every nation he that feareth God, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.
Accepted by all religions. The Qur’an names Jews, Christians and Sabaeans beside the believers: whoever doeth right, no fear shall come upon them.
Spiritual education causes “competition in praiseworthy actions”. The Qur’an: vie with one another in good works.
The message is delivered through goodly deeds and “the happiness reflected from the face” of the one who speaks. Whitman: we do not convince by arguments; we convince by our presence.
“The deeds of the teacher should attest the truth of his words.” Confucius on the superior man: he acts before he speaks, and afterwards speaks according to his actions.
Deeds first, then utterance. Paul’s charge to a young teacher: be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity.
The Bahá’ís “must first be implementers of the teachings”. The proverb Jesus expected to hear: Physician, heal thyself.
How can one who has not found existence give it to others? The Dhammapada: let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others.
“The influence of deeds is more potent than the influence of words.” The Dhammapada: fine words without action are a flower full of colour but without scent.
Deeds are each “a herald of truth”. Shammai in the Mishnah: speak little, but do much.
“One pure deed shall transcend the heavens.” Portia, coming home at night: how far that little candle throws his beams! So shines a good deed in a naughty world.
Goodly deeds and character are “the hosts of God”, a weapon that unlocks the gates of cities. Paul: the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty to the pulling down of strong holds.

“Goodly deeds and praiseworthy character are sharper than swords.” Machiavelli read history otherwise: all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed. What would each of them count as victory?
The influence of pure deeds “cannot be weakened by the power of the world’s armies”. Zechariah: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
Victory is ordained “through wisdom and utterance, and through deeds and character”. Jesus, to a disciple with a drawn sword: put up again thy sword into his place.
“Aid ye your Lord through goodly character — through this His Cause is exalted.” The Sermon on the Mount: let your light so shine, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father.
Service to the Cause “consists of goodly deeds and praiseworthy human actions”. Micah’s answer to the same question: to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly.
Through goodly deeds “the standards of victory [shall] be hoisted upon every lofty mountain”. Jesus: a city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
“Blessed are they that act, and woe unto them that neglect.” James: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Woe to those who neglect. Mill told a university that bad men need nothing more to compass their ends than that good men should look on and do nothing.
“Counsel the servants through deeds and character.” Confucius: the superior man is modest in his speech, but exceeds in his actions.
Counsel given by conduct. Paul calls his converts a letter of that kind: our epistle, known and read of all men.
“Deeds are more potent than words.” Roosevelt: it is not the critic who counts; the credit belongs to the man who is actually in the arena.
“Through one goodly deed … an entire kingdom … became illumined.” Jesus’ parable of small beginnings: the least of all seeds becomes a tree.
People are to “discover the Source through the manners and conduct of these souls”. Tertullian records pagans doing so: see, they say, how they love one another.

“A righteous deed is, in itself, a teacher of God’s Cause.” Thoreau would run for his life from a man coming with the conscious design of doing him good. When does a good deed done in order to teach stop being a good deed?
“We are ourselves the means of our degradation and exaltation.” Paul: whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
People are drawn or repelled by what emanates from us. Cassius: the fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, but in ourselves.
Our attributes and deeds decide how we stand. Heraclitus said it in four words: man’s character is his fate.
“Your deeds must be so holy and pure that they will be even as the sun amidst the works of creation.” Daniel: they that turn many to righteousness shall shine as the stars.
Every action that elevates the Word of God is accepted: “This is the standard.” Paul’s standard: whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.

“Sometimes there is dismissal and sometimes appointment … What matters are deeds.” Kipling asks for the same steadiness without mentioning God: meet with Triumph and Disaster and treat those two impostors just the same. What holds a person steady in each case?
Nothing in this world continues; deeds are what matter. The Preacher draws the same conclusion from the same premise: whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might.
One pleasing deed outweighs “seas of elixir and the treasures of the world”. Jesus watched a widow put in two mites and said she had given more than all.
“Pure deeds reveal themselves and open their own door.” Jesus asks that alms be so secret the left hand does not know. Should a good deed be seen, as much of this guide hopes, or hidden?
“A good deed hath a pleasing reward, for the Judge of Justice is God.” Hebrews: God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love.
“No deed hath been or ever shall be concealed … All are recorded and inscribed in the Divine Book.” John’s vision: the books were opened, and the dead were judged according to their works.
“The reward of thy deeds is remembered and treasured with God.” The angel to a Roman officer: thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God.
One breath drawn in the path of the Friend is recorded. Jesus on the smallest gift: a cup of cold water only shall in no wise lose its reward.
“That which endureth and lasteth is a deed … in the path of God.” Revelation on the dead: they rest from their labours, and their works do follow them.
Bahá’u’lláh says that what lasts is the good deed. Antony, over Caesar’s body: the evil that men do lives after them; the good is oft interred with their bones. Which does the world remember?
Deeds done in the path of God endure. Shelley’s king left an inscription inviting the mighty to look on his works, and round it the lone and level sands. What kind of work outlasts its maker?
“Whatsoever pure word and holy deed proceedeth from anyone shall endure.” George Eliot ends Middlemarch on the same faith: the growing good of the world depends on unhistoric acts.
The reader is to strive for deeds whose fragrance endures through earth and heaven. The Preacher looked on all the works his hands had wrought, and all was vanity. What had his works been for?
Every deed done purely for God “is adorned with the ornament of perpetuity”. Paul: your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
“The day of deeds hath come: Now is not the time for words.” Jesus: I must work while it is day; the night cometh, when no man can work.
“Blessed are they who … act according to that which hath been sent down.” Jesus’ parable of two sons, one who said yes and did not go, one who said no and went.
“Aid your Lord through goodly deeds.” The Qur’an: Act! God will behold your actions.

Every deed done for God’s sake is recorded “as the lord of deeds”. Paul expects a harder audit: every man’s work shall be tried by fire, of what sort it is. Which deeds would a person want tested that way?
“Know thou its worth and act in a manner befitting it.” Brutus: there is a tide in the affairs of men, which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune.
This is the Day. Hillel’s three questions end on the same point: and if not now, when?
“Today is the Day of deeds.” Longfellow’s schoolroom lines: let us, then, be up and doing, with a heart for any fate.
The day of deeds. Rabbi Tarfon: the day is short, and the work is plentiful, and the master of the house is insistent.

Hold fast to deeds, “that perchance His mercy may take them by the hand”. Paul holds effort and grace in one sentence: work out your own salvation, for it is God which worketh in you. Who is doing the work?
What is beloved “hath ever been and will ever be goodly deeds and praiseworthy character”. The Preacher’s last word: this is the whole duty of man, for God shall bring every work into judgment.
“A goodly deed is acceptable, and a goodly word ascendeth unto God.” The sentence echoes this verse of the Qur’an: unto Him good words ascend, and the pious deed doth He exalt.

james-shew-me-thy-faith.text: Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works

luke-why-call-ye-me-lord.text: And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say

revelation-books-were-opened.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works

proverbs-child-known-by-his-doings.text: Even a child is known by his doings, whether his work be pure, and whether it be right

corinthians-fire-shall-try.text: Every man's work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is

galatians-whatsoever-a-man-soweth.text: Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap

philippians-work-out-your-own-salvation.text: Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure

romans-doers-of-the-law.text: For not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified

isaiah-filthy-rags.text: But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags; and we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away

amos-let-judgment-run-down.text: I hate, I despise your feast days, and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies. Though ye offer me burnt offerings and your meat offerings, I will not accept them: neither will I regard the peace offerings of your fat beasts. Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols. But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream

ecclesiastes-all-the-works-my-hands.text: Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun

matthew-tree-is-known-by-his-fruit.text: Either make the tree good, and his fruit good; or else make the tree corrupt, and his fruit corrupt: for the tree is known by his fruit. O generation of vipers, how can ye, being evil, speak good things? for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh. A good man out of the good treasure of the heart bringeth forth good things: and an evil man out of the evil treasure bringeth forth evil things

quran-good-words-ascend.text: Whoso desireth power (should know that) all power belongeth to Allah. Unto Him good words ascend, and the pious deed doth He exalt; but those who plot iniquities, theirs will be an awful doom; and the plotting of such (folk) will come to naught.

quran-do-righteous-work.text: Say: I am only a mortal like you. My Lord inspireth in me that your Allah is only One Allah. And whoever hopeth for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work, and make none sharer of the worship due unto his Lord.

shakespeare-if-to-do-were-as-easy.text: If to do were as easy as to know what were good to do, chapels had been churches and poor men's cottages princes' palaces. It is a good divine that follows his own instructions: I can easier teach twenty what were good to be done, than be one of the twenty to follow mine own teaching

dhammapada-flower-without-scent.text: Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly. But, like a beautiful flower, full of colour and full of scent, are the fine and fruitful words of him who acts accordingly

carlyle-conviction-into-conduct.text: Conviction, were it never so excellent, is worthless till it convert itself into Conduct

analects-hear-words-look-at-conduct.text: At first, my way with men was to hear their words, and give them credit for their conduct. Now my way is to hear their words, and look at their conduct

aristotle-take-refuge-in-theory.text: But most people do not do these, but take refuge in theory and think they are being philosophers and will become good in this way
